newsitem.title: INDIA: Embattled India Hindu party ponders new strategies.
newsitem.headline: Embattled India Hindu party ponders new strategies.

text.p: India's main nationalist party, dogged by image problems and internal dissent, met on Friday at the start of a three-day conclave near Bombay to assess its performance and chalk out future plans, party members said.

After a tumultuous year which saw it take power for just 12 days in the wake of inconclusive general elections in May, about 32 of the Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) top leaders gathered to evaluate its prospects.
"It will be a process of churning, thoughtful churning," said the party's general secretary Sharad Kulkarni.
"It will be an in-depth review of various party programmes and policies during the year -- where things went wrong, what the achievements were," he added.

There were troubling times in 1996 for the BJP. The party projected itself as a viable alternative to the scandal-ridden Congress party, which ruled India for much of the nation's independent history.
But the BJP's hold on federal power last year ended swiftly, after it failed to entice other major parties into an alliance to clinch a parliamentary majority.
Internal dissent has plagued the BJP, leading to the downfall of its government in western Gujarat state, and difficulties for its government in the desert state of Rajasthan.

"The MLAs (Members of Legislative Assembly) in Rajasthan are being bought and they are selling themselves," said BJP leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee, India's prime minister for a brief period last year. He accused the Congress of playing a key role in pulling down the BJP in Gujarat.
The BJP, in alliance with the regional Shiv Sena, rules India's wealthiest state of Maharashtra, where detractors have accused deputy chief minister Gopinath Munde of corruption.
"The new year is full of challenges for BJP-ruled states, but the party will foil all plots to remove it," Vajpayee told reporters before the meeting began.
The party suffered another blow in October, when it was unable to win an outright majority in elections for the assembly of Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state.

The BJP won 177 of the 425 seats in the state, but Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ruling United Front alliance secured 134 seats. The Congress party, fighting the polls on a common plank with the low-caste Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), won 100.
Any party or coalition had to win at least 213 seats to stake a claim to forming a new Uttar Pradesh government.
Since then, the political situation in Uttar Pradesh, which the BJP hoped would be its springboard to national power, has been in a stalemate, with no group able to form a government.
"The one-point programme of rival parties is to keep the BJP out of power," party president Lal Krishan Advani said.

General secretary Kulkarni said the BJP was hoping to entice the BSP into an alliance to form the Uttar Pradesh government. The meeting, at Bombay's suburb of Virar will evaluate the progress of the BJP's negotiations with the BSP. "The party's ongoing talks with the BSP, for a possible alliance to form the government in Uttar Pradesh, as well as the party's future line of action will be discussed," he said.
Another line of attack for the BJP leaders is the nation's economic difficulties, Kulkarni said.

"The hike in the inflation rate, which has reached a record 7.58 percent, the drastic fall in exports, and the move towards full convertibility of the rupee are some issues which will dominate the discussions," he said.
Leaders of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu right-wing organisation from which the BJP draws its ideological sustenance, are also attending the meeting, BJP members said.
